title: Two Views of the Same Transformation September 15, 2026 of-the-Same-Transformation.pdf
author: Jen Weedon, Megan McDermott, and Sara Berger
source: All Tech Is Human x Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics Lab (alltechishuman.org),
summary: This white paper from All Tech Is Human and the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics Lab reports on paired July 2026 workshops in New York that asked 45 mid-level professionals and 30 executives mirrored questions about how generative and agentic AI are changing work. Its central argument is that technical deployment is outpacing organizational and human adaptation, and that the two cohorts describe the same transformation through very different instruments. Across both groups, speed and productivity have become de facto values, 'good enough' work at roughly 60% of expert quality is becoming the baseline, and productivity gains convert into higher expectations rather than returned time. The report documents invisible labor, including validating AI outputs and the 'glue work' of training, translating strategy, and managing anxiety, which is absent from job descriptions and performance reviews and sometimes falls disproportionately on women. Executives measured adoption mainly by usage and speed and questioned the need for middle management, even as they feared 'distributed deskilling,' the loss of mentoring and apprenticeship that middle managers largely provide. The paper closes with recommendations for leaders to audit what their metrics miss, make validation and glue work visible, localize adoption decisions, and protect valued work done by hand.
points: Executives defaulted to usage, speed, and efficiency metrics that omit validation, translation, mentoring, and coordination, so organizations may be measuring what they can rather than what matters.
When organizations accept LLM-assisted generalist work at about 60% of expert quality, expertise shifts from a baseline standard to an undervalued premium.
Validating AI outputs and the 'glue work' of adoption are critical to successful change yet remain invisible in job descriptions and reviews.

Leaders questioning the need for middle management were simultaneously worried about 'distributed deskilling,' a paradox since middle managers perform much of the mentoring and knowledge transfer at risk.

Methodologically, mid-level participants readily described grief and identity loss while executives stayed in strategy language, suggesting strategy-framed inquiries systematically obscure human costs.
quotes: Both described the same broad shifts: AI is not simply automating tasks, but reconfiguring the lived experience of work itself, with technical deployments currently outpacing organizational and human adaptation.

Across both cohorts, speed and productivity have become de facto organizational values; “good enough” is increasingly accepted as a new baseline; and productivity gains rapidly convert into higher expectations instead of the promise of returned capacity.

When discussing how they evaluated AI adoption, executives regularly defaulted to usage, speed, and efficiency—metrics that largely exclude the work of validation, translation, mentoring, coordination, and managing team anxieties.

Many of the very skillsets executives expressed fear of losing were already being performed, albeit often invisibly, by the organizational layer of middle management, whose future they were beginning to question. Organizations may value these functions in principle while relying on metrics that fail to capture them, and a tier whose primary contributions sit outside the formal measurement system will inevitably appear costly relative to its measured output.

This speaks to one of the questions that spurred this research, which is that decision makers and those implementing and experiencing their decisions do not always describe the same organizational reality. This is not necessarily because either is wrong, but because the instruments organizations use to understand themselves can make one cohort’s most valuable work difficult for the other to see.

These differences matter methodologically: asking organizations about AI transformation primarily through the language of strategy, productivity, and change management may systematically obscure some of its most consequential human effects.

Several groups observed that when organizations routinely accept LLM-assisted generalist work at 60% of expert quality, they effectively turn expertise from a baseline standard into a premium. Participants shared they believe that organizations still need subject matter expertise, but that the expertise is undervalued or reduced to its value for model training inputs.

Whether the emphasis on productivity in current metrics reflects an intentional definition of productivity as synonymous with success, or simply emerged as something that simply can be measured went unexamined. In other words, as reported by participants, organizations may be measuring what they can, rather than what matters, if the latter is even defined.
